newsitem.title: INDIA: India firms to guarantee naphtha for power plants.
newsitem.headline: India firms to guarantee naphtha for power plants.

text.p: Indian oil companies will be asked to provide guarantees on supplies of liquid fuels, especially naphtha, to power producers to ensure uninterrupted generation, a Petroleum Ministry official said on Friday.
The nation's ports and railways will in turn be asked to guarantee the oil firms timely and adequate movements of fuel, the official, who did not wish to be identified, told Reuters.
The back-to-back guarantees to power firms will be applicable so long as the power projects ensure compliance with safety and pollution norms, he said.
"The decision to provide back-to-back guarantee on supply was taken by an inter-ministerial commitee of senior most officers on July 10," he said.

To ensure smooth imports and movement of liquid fuels, the state-run oil companies will construct three additional jetties -- one each at Kandla in the western state of Gujarat, Ennore in the southern state of Tamil Nadu and at Mangalore in the southwestern state of Karnataka, the official said.
In addition, one jetty each at Kakinada in the southern state of Andhra Pradesh and at Mudbidri in Karnataka will be developed by the respective state governments.
"The government agreed to developing the Paradeep port in Orissa to supplement the Kandla port," the official said.

The Ministry of Surface Transport has been asked to provide land to oil companies to construct storage tanks for providing a minimum 15 days supply cover. "The power producers will be asked to put up storage facilities for a 30-day cover," he said.

The government has also decided that all power plants should be designed for multi-fuel operation and commercial arrangements with oil firms will provide for alternative fuel supplies, the official said.
Power producers will have the option to import liquid fuels on their own and to opt out of fuel supply agreements with oil firms.
"Licences for import of naphtha will be given freely but strict conditions will be laid down so that its end use is protected," he said.
The government has decided to warn power producers of the likelihood of a change in the import tariff on naphtha which does not attract any duty currently, the official said.
"Potential users need to be warned about the overall shortage of naphtha so that they can take proper commercial and technological decisions," he said.

In order to bridge the large gap in electricity demand projections and installed power generation capacity, India in late 1995 approved the setting up of short-gestation power projects based on liquid fuels such as naphtha, fuel oil and low sulphur heavy stock.

The response for putting up naphtha-based power projects was overwhelming and the government had to restrict fuel linkages to 12,000 megawatts of generation capacity as it would translate into additional imports of about 20 million tonnes of naphtha.

Fearing a spurt in the international price of naphtha due to the additional imports, the Petroleum Ministry proposed that naphtha be kept out of the government's administered price regime and said prices must be based on import-parity cost.
The current price of naphtha excluding excise duty in India is 6,683.26 rupees ($187.2) per tonne whereas the international price for August cargos is being quoted at $191.50-192.00 per tonne.
